title: Meeting overrun hourglass
hero: graphite-framed hourglass
start: A single hourglass about the height of a coffee cup stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Its frame is matte graphite metal with four slim turned pillars and chamfered end caps. The bulbs are sandblasted-frosted at the rims and clear in the middle. The upper bulb holds fine ivory sand, and a thin band of acid-lime sand marks one booked hour that is just about to run through. To the right, five ivory paper calendar blocks stand upright on a slim graphite rail, evenly spaced like dominoes waiting their turn, each a thick folded card with a crisp spine and blank face. The falling thread of sand is sharp and fine, and a faint dust of grains rests on the base plate. Everything is orderly, quiet and precisely aligned.
end: The same graphite hourglass now leans forward on its base with the lower bulb overflowing. Pale ivory sand pours in a continuous stream over the base plate and spreads across the tabletop in a soft rippled drift. The lime band has long since run through and lies buried under ivory sand in the lower bulb. The drift has reached the calendar rail: the first two blocks are half buried and leaning, the third is being shoved sideways and creasing at its spine, and the last is caught mid-fall off the table edge with a fine curtain of sand pouring after it. Airborne grains catch the light, a thin haze of dust hangs over the drift, and ripples in the sand run straight back to the hourglass.
apocalypse: A vast miniature desert of pale ivory sand dunes rolls to a hazy horizon, seen from a low, wide viewpoint. Half buried in the nearest dune lies the building-sized fallen frame of a graphite hourglass. One pillar is snapped, and the frosted bulbs are cracked and packed with sand. Around it, the tops of ivory calendar blocks jut from the dunes like weathered monoliths, tilted and broken, their spines bleached and frayed. Wind ripples cross the sand. In the middle distance, a slim graphite sieve conveyor with lime-painted buckets climbs one dune, lifting sand into a rotating frosted drum and dropping small recovered lime tokens into a neat tray. A second graphite rig stakes a taut lime survey line from the drum back to the fallen frame.

title: Recurring meeting zombie
hero: graphite invite spindle with stamping arm
start: A brushed graphite desk spindle about the height of a pencil stands on a heavy round base at the left of a pale neutral tabletop, with a single ivory invite card pressed onto its spike, crisp-edged and blank. Behind the spindle sits a small hinged stamping arm, its flat graphite foot resting still. To the right, an ivory card archive box about the size of a shoebox is closed and tied with pale paper twine, its lid sealed with a plain frosted acrylic tab. On the spindle base, an acid-lime repeat dial, a thumb-sized knurled wheel, is still switched on, the only sign the series never ended. A fine film of dust lies on the box lid, and the base shows light machining rings. Everything is square and still.
end: The same graphite spindle is now buried under its own output. The stamping arm is caught mid-strike, pressing another identical ivory invite card onto a stack that has climbed far past the spike and leans against the back wall in a tall, bowing column. The acid-lime repeat dial is still on, blurred mid-rotation. Loose cards shoot sideways from the base, fanning across the tabletop and piling against the sealed archive box, which has been shoved to the right, its twine taut and its lid lifting at one corner. Several cards hang frozen in the air between the press and the box, flat and spinning. Dented corners, creases and fine paper dust mark the path back to the spindle.
apocalypse: A deep open quarry is cut into compressed strata of ivory invite cards, its terraced walls showing thousands of thin layers pressed into grey-white bands under a pale sky. On the pit floor rises the building-sized graphite spindle, bent a few degrees off vertical, its spike dulled and scratched, its stamping arm snapped and lying across two terraces. The archive box, now the size of a warehouse, is crushed flat into one wall and shows only as a buckled ivory edge between layers. Card flakes drift in shallow piles along the ledges, and the quarry rim fades into haze. At the spindle's root, a slim graphite gantry rig with a lime circular saw blade and lime clamp jaws has cut halfway through the shaft, leaving a clean bright kerf and a fan of metal filings below.

title: Time-zone math
hero: three graphite desk clocks on a shared rail
start: Three round desk clocks stand in a shallow arc across a pale neutral tabletop, each about the size of a saucer on a short graphite foot. Their cases are brushed graphite with chamfered bezels, and their faces are frosted acrylic with plain tick marks and slim graphite hands, each set to a different hour. A narrow graphite rail links the three bases, and on it rides a single ivory meeting card in a small sliding carriage, halfway between the left and centre clocks. The card's acid-lime edge strip marks the one slot that suits everyone. Behind each clock, a small frosted glass dome glows faintly warm, bright or dim to suggest morning, noon and night. Fine dust sits in the rail groove. Everything is aligned and quiet.
end: The same three clocks are now locked together. The centre clock has tipped left, and its minute hand has hooked over its neighbour's hand; both frosted faces are cracked straight across. The right clock's back plate has sprung open, and small graphite gears spill across the tabletop, rolling mid-motion toward the rail. The rail itself has bowed, and the meeting card's carriage has been dragged past every clock into the far end under the dim dome, where the card is bent double, its acid-lime edge strip creased and half hidden. A snapped spring, loose gear teeth and a fine haze of metal dust hang frozen in the air, and scrape marks on the tabletop lead back to the hooked hands.
apocalypse: A dim, flat plain of pale grey grit stretches to a low horizon under a dusky sky, with long shadows running across it. Three toppled clock towers lie at wide intervals, each the size of a lighthouse: graphite cases split open, frosted faces shattered into milky shards, hands bent and pointing in different directions. Loose gears as large as cartwheels lie half sunk in the grit in a scattered trail. The bowed rail runs between the towers in broken sections, and the meeting card survives as a weathered ivory slab folded over one of them. Across the middle ground, a slim graphite rail-laying rig is setting a single straight drive shaft from the nearest tower toward the next, fitting lime gear couplings at each joint, and the second tower's axle has already begun to turn.

title: No-agenda meeting
hero: model meeting table with a blank agenda sheet
start: A model meeting table about the length of a ruler sits in the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, built from brushed graphite with a thin frosted acrylic top that glows softly from inside. Six small graphite chairs are tucked evenly around it. At the exact centre of the table lies one ivory agenda sheet, crisp-edged and completely blank, held flat by a small acid-lime paperweight cube, the one thing everyone should be looking at. From each chair, a thin frosted glass tube runs toward the sheet, but every tube stops short of it. An empty frosted glass tumbler stands at the far end beside a folded ivory card. Fine dust lies on the chair seats and fibres show at the sheet's edge. The layout is symmetrical and still.
end: The same table has stretched to several times its length, its graphite frame pulled apart at new joints and extra frosted panels caught sliding into the gaps. More graphite chairs are skidding in from both sides, some still tipping as they land. The frosted glass tubes have grown into long loops that curve from seat to seat, over and under one another and around the chair backs, but none of them reaches the centre. There, the blank agenda sheet is still pinned by its acid-lime cube, untouched, with a faint ring of dust around it. Ivory note cards have spilled from the loops and hang in the air, the tumbler has toppled, and scuff marks on the tabletop trace the table's outward slide from the original frame.
apocalypse: A wide overgrown plain of pale grasses and low scrub rolls to a misty horizon. Across it lies a maze of broken frosted glass tubes, each now as thick as a culvert pipe, looping and doubling back through the grass, cracked, clouded and wrapped in vines. The graphite table frame, as long as a runway, sags between them on bent legs, and the chair frames stand in rows like weathered fence posts. At the centre of the maze, the agenda sheet has become a flat, bleached ivory plaza, still blank and bare. A slim graphite survey crawler on low tracks is laying one straight track from the edge of the maze to the plaza, driving lime survey stakes at even intervals and cutting cleanly through each loop it crosses with a lime cutting wheel.

title: Wrong window screen-share
hero: graphite laptop and pocket projector
start: A small graphite laptop about the size of a paperback sits open at the left of a pale neutral tabletop, its screen a blank frosted acrylic panel glowing softly. A narrow beam of light runs from a tiny graphite projector beside it to a small frosted glass screen on a stand at the right, where it lands as one soft, even rectangle. Tucked half out of sight behind the laptop stands a neat stack of ivory draft sheets and a folded private note card. The laptop's acid-lime share switch, a tiny toggle on the hinge, is flipped on. A light film of dust sits on the projector's lens housing, and the draft stack has one dog-eared corner. Everything is tidy and centred, and the beam is clean and narrow.
end: The same projector beam has split into several wide, uneven fans of light reaching in every direction. The ivory draft sheets behind the laptop have been blown out of their stack and are flying through the beams, each throwing a large blank rectangular shadow onto the frosted screen, the tabletop and the back wall. The private note card has flipped open in mid-air. The frosted screen has tipped back on its stand, and two more frosted glass panels have toppled from behind it, one cracked across the corner. The laptop's acid-lime share switch is still flipped on. Fine dust glitters in the beams, and loose sheets slide across the table away from the projector, their paths fanning out from the laptop.
apocalypse: A white salt flat stretches to a flat, shimmering horizon, its crust broken into hexagonal plates. Thousands of broken frosted glass panes the size of barn doors lie scattered and half embedded in the crust, tilted at every angle and catching a flat grey light. At the left, the laptop has become a collapsed graphite pavilion, its lid snapped off the hinge and lying face down in the salt, and the projector lies beside it as a split graphite block. Weathered ivory sheets, stiff and salt-stained, are pinned beneath the panes. In the middle distance, a slim graphite crane on a rail cart lifts one clean frosted pane with lime suction cups and lowers it into a lime-edged frame, the first in a straight row of re-seated panes running back toward the pavilion.

title: Frozen video call
hero: frosted acrylic video tile on a desk stand
start: A slim graphite desk stand at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop holds a single square frosted acrylic video tile, about the size of a drink mat, glowing a soft, even white. A small graphite webcam on a short jointed arm faces it from the left, its lens ring machined with fine concentric lines. To the right, a row of four more frosted tiles leans in a shallow graphite rack, dim and waiting their turn. The webcam's acid-lime status ring, a thin band around the lens, is lit. A faint cold haze drifts across the lead tile's surface. Light dust rests on the rack, and one of the waiting tiles carries a small scuff. All objects sit square and evenly spaced.
end: The same frosted video tile has iced over completely. A thick crust of rime covers its face and runs down the stand, and frost fingers reach sideways along the rack, fusing the four neighbouring tiles into one cloudy block. Long clear icicles hang from the underside of the stand and the rack, some reaching the tabletop, one snapped mid-fall with fragments bouncing off the table. The webcam's acid-lime status ring still glows through a skin of frost on its arm, which has stiffened at an angle. A patch of hoarfrost creeps across the tabletop from the stand's foot, and fine ice crystals hang frozen in the air. Every frost line traces back to the lead tile at the centre.
apocalypse: A long glacier fills a steep mountain valley under a pale overcast sky, its surface ribbed with blue-white crevasses. Fused frosted acrylic tiles the size of buildings are locked in the ice, stacked and tilted, their milky edges showing through the glacier like layered stone. Near its snout, the graphite desk stand juts out as a bent tower, and the webcam arm lies snapped across a moraine of grey gravel and ice blocks. Meltwater streaks run down the valley walls. From the valley mouth, a slim graphite sled rig on long skis pays out lime heating cable across the ice from a lime drum, melting a narrow, straight channel of clear water toward the stand; the channel steams faintly and its edges are clean and glassy.

title: Double-booked room
hero: miniature frosted conference room
start: A miniature conference room model about the size of a shoebox sits at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, with frosted acrylic walls, a brushed graphite frame and a narrow door in the front face. Inside, one graphite table and four chairs are arranged neatly. Clipped to the doorframe are two blank ivory booking tabs, overlapping by half their width, pinched together by a small acid-lime clip, the only hint of a problem. To the left and right, two small graphite trays each hold a folded ivory meeting pack, one for each booking. Dust sits along the door sill, and the frosted walls carry faint water marks. Everything is square, centred and calm.
end: The same room is now holding two meetings at once. From the left, a second graphite table has been shoved through the doorway and rammed into the first, the two tabletops overlapping and lifting off their legs. Chairs from both setups are jammed together, one tipped over mid-fall, another wedged against a wall. The frosted acrylic walls bow outward, and a hairline crack runs up one corner. Both meeting packs have burst from their trays, and ivory sheets fly out through the doorway. The acid-lime clip still pinches the two booking tabs, now bent sideways by the door, which has sprung off one hinge. Scrape marks and paper dust trace the push from the left.
apocalypse: A wide dry riverbed of pale gravel and flat stones runs toward low hills under a thin, bright sky. In its middle lies the conference room, now the size of an office block and crushed flat: frosted acrylic walls shattered into milky plates, the graphite frame folded like a collapsed trellis. The two enormous tables lie wrecked on top of each other, legs pointing skyward, bleached and scoured by old floods. Ivory sheets have weathered into stiff papery crusts across the stones, and the door lies flat some distance downstream. Across the site, a slim graphite rail-laying machine moves along a narrow track, setting lime partition rails into the gravel in a clean grid of bays; the first bay is already cleared, with one intact table set squarely inside it.

title: Quick call that isn't
hero: folded paper concertina call chip
start: A long brushed graphite day strip about the length of a forearm runs left to right across a pale neutral tabletop, with shallow slots along its top edge. Near the left end sits one small ivory paper chip, folded into a tight concertina no wider than a matchbox, its pleats crisp and even. An acid-lime tab on its leading end marks the short call that was booked. Further along the strip, a frosted acrylic lunch block and two ivory focus blocks sit in their slots, evenly spaced with open gaps between them. A graphite end stop caps the right end. Fine paper fibres show along the chip's folds, and light dust sits in the empty slots. The day looks open and uncluttered.
end: The same concertina chip has unfolded along the entire day strip. Its pleats have opened into a long zigzag of ivory paper that fills every slot, rising and sagging as it goes. As it expanded it shoved the frosted lunch block and both focus blocks to the right, where they are piled against the graphite end stop; one focus block has flipped over, and the lunch block is caught mid-fall over the side of the strip. The acid-lime tab is still at the leading edge of the unfolding paper, pressed hard against the pile. Loose pleats bow upward, a torn corner flutters in the air, and creases and paper dust along the strip lead back to the chip's starting slot.
apocalypse: A range of low terraced hills rolls to a hazy horizon, every slope formed from vast weathered pleats of ivory paper, stiffened and greyed at the folds, with scrub growing in the creases. At the far end, the graphite day strip lies as a long broken ridge wall, and the lunch and focus blocks are tumbled boulders the size of houses, cracked and bleached, heaped against the end stop. Wind has frayed the pleat edges into fibrous fringes. On the nearest slope, a slim graphite cutter rig runs on a short rail, slicing the unfolded paper into clean, even segments with a lime wire blade and stacking each section on a lime-edged pallet; the first recovered short block sits squarely in its own restored slot.

title: Lost action items
hero: open notebook with action-item cards
start: An open ivory notebook about the size of a paperback lies on a model meeting table at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop; the table has a brushed graphite frame and a frosted acrylic top. Three small blank ivory action-item cards are tucked into the notebook's spine, crisp-edged. The top card has an acid-lime corner, the task that matters most. Beside the notebook lie a slim graphite pen and a folded ivory agenda. At the table's near edge, a narrow gap where two frosted panels meet is just visible as a thin dark line. Light dust sits on the table, and the notebook pages show soft fibre and a faint crease. Everything is neat and square.
end: The same notebook has slid toward the gap between the frosted panels, its spine tipped downward. The three action-item cards have slipped out: one is wedged halfway into the gap, one is falling through it into a narrow frosted glass chute that angles down beneath the table toward the floor, and the acid-lime card is tumbling end over end at the chute's mouth. The graphite pen is rolling after them, and the folded agenda has slid over the table edge. Loose pages lift from the notebook in the draught. A thin trail of paper dust runs along the chute, and a scuffed path on the frosted top traces the slide back to where the notebook began.
apocalypse: A deep circular pit opens in a scrubby plain, its walls lined with packed layers of lost ivory cards, bleached and stiff, sliding like scree down to the floor far below. On its rim stands the collapsed meeting table, now the size of a tower block, its graphite legs buckled and its frosted panels cracked, with the broken chute hanging down into the pit like a dry spillway. The notebook lies splayed open on a ledge, its pages fused together. Beside the chute, a slim graphite retrieval crane reaches its long boom down into the pit; its lime claw is lifting one intact card out of the drift, and a lime conveyor carries recovered cards up to a neat stack on the rim. Distant scrub fades into haze.

title: Waiting-room limbo
hero: miniature lobby with a pending tile
start: A small lobby model about the size of a shoebox sits at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, with a frosted acrylic back wall, a brushed graphite floor and a closed frosted glass door at the right. In front of the door, one small blank ivory pending tile stands upright on a graphite base, waiting. Two slim graphite stanchions joined by a pale paper rope mark the queue lane. Above the door, a small round acid-lime indicator lens on a graphite bracket sits unlit, the signal that never comes. An empty frosted tumbler stands on a side ledge. Fine dust gathers along the base of the door. The lobby is quiet, clean and orderly.
end: The same lobby door is still closed. Behind the first pending tile, dozens of identical ivory tiles now stand in a line held between graphite stanchions and pale paper ropes, the queue doubling back on itself, spilling out of the lobby, running to the edge of the tabletop and over it onto the floor. Near the edge, several tiles are frozen mid-topple like dominoes, and one stanchion is tipping with its rope pulled taut. The acid-lime indicator above the door is still unlit. Tiles at the back of the line lean against one another, and a trail of small scuff marks and paper dust runs along the queue back to the door.
apocalypse: A long valley filled with low fog stretches away between dim hills, with visibility fading within a short distance. Across its floor runs a field of weathered graphite stanchions, some upright, many leaning or snapped, with sagging grey paper ropes strung between them in endless switchbacks. Ivory pending tiles the size of standing stones lie toppled in long rows, lichen spotting their faces. At the far end, the lobby has become a bleached ruin, its frosted back wall cracked and its door frame bare. A slim graphite gate rig has been bolted into that frame; its lime hinge arms are swinging one new frosted gate open, and a lime guide rail runs from the gate out into the fog along the first row of tiles.

title: Out-of-office loop
hero: two facing graphite mail trays
start: Two brushed graphite mail trays sit facing each other at the left and right of a pale neutral tabletop, about a paperback's length apart, each the size of a paperback. In each tray rests a single ivory envelope, sealed, crisp and blank. Between them runs a short frosted acrylic chute, open at both ends, so either tray can send to the other. On the left tray's rim, a small acid-lime auto-reply toggle is switched on. Behind the right tray, a tiny graphite chair is pushed in with a folded blank ivory card standing on its seat, a sign its owner is away. Light dust lies in the chute. Everything is aligned and quiet.
end: The same two trays are now firing at each other. Envelopes shoot through the frosted chute in both directions, several caught mid-air at its midpoint, colliding and spinning. Each tray is spitting out a new envelope as another lands, and the overflow has built into a dense, sloping pile of ivory envelopes that fills the gap between them and spills off the front of the table. The acid-lime toggle on the left tray is still on, blurred by vibration. The chute has cracked along one side, and the tiny chair behind the right tray has tipped over, its card lying face down. Paper dust hangs in the air, and fresh scuffs show the trays juddering apart.
apocalypse: A narrow gorge runs between two sheer cliff walls, each crowned by a ruined graphite fortress: the two mail trays grown enormous and split open at their rims. Between them, deep drifts of weathered ivory envelopes fill the gorge floor like wind-packed snow, flaps curled, edges softened into fibre. The frosted chute spans the gap high overhead as a cracked, sagging bridge, with envelopes still jammed inside it. Cloud shadows cross the far cliff faces. At the centre of the gorge, a slim graphite tripod rig stands on the drift, lowering a lime cut-off valve into the broken chute on a cable; its lime handwheel is half turned, and on the downstream side the chute is already clear and empty.

title: CC creep
hero: envelope launch cradle and frosted delivery tube
start: At the left of a pale neutral tabletop, one ivory envelope sits in a small brushed graphite launch cradle. From the cradle, a single frosted glass delivery tube about as thick as a pencil runs straight across the table to one graphite mail slot mounted on a short stand at the right. Where the tube meets the cradle it is fitted with an acid-lime collar, the joint where extra copies can be added. The envelope is crisp, blank and flat. Behind the slot, a row of other graphite slots stands unused and capped. Light dust lies along the tube, and the cradle shows fine machining lines. The route is clean and direct.
end: The same frosted tube has split at the acid-lime collar into many branches. New tubes fork again and again, fanning across the tabletop to every capped slot and beyond, some stretching off the table edge. Inside them, the single envelope has divided into dozens of identical copies, frozen mid-travel in every branch, and more copies spill out of open junctions and flutter onto the table. The original slot at the right receives only a crumpled corner. Several tubes have cracked at their joints, with small puffs of paper dust escaping, and the capped slots have popped their caps. The branching pattern traces clearly back to the collar at the cradle.
apocalypse: A wide, pale marsh spreads to a flat horizon, shallow water between grass tussocks reflecting a grey sky. Across it lies a collapsed fan of enormous frosted glass tubes, each as wide as a road, snapped and draped over hummocks, their ends sunk in the mud. Weathered ivory envelopes, sodden and grey, are wedged in broken sections and silted into the shallows. The launch cradle stands as a tilted graphite pier at the left, and the single mail slot rises as a leaning tower far to the right. A slim graphite crawler on long jointed legs steps across the marsh, laying one straight new frosted tube on lime support trestles from the cradle toward the slot, its lime clamps closing each joint.

title: Subject-line fork
hero: graphite rail carrying an envelope thread
start: A single narrow graphite rail about the length of a ruler runs across a pale neutral tabletop from left to right. On it, a neat thread of ivory envelopes rides in small graphite carriages, nose to tail, each envelope crisp and blank. Just ahead of the lead carriage, a small graphite switch point sits in the rail, closed, its lever resting flat. One envelope in the middle of the thread has an acid-lime folded corner, the reply that changes the subject. At the right, the rail ends against a single frosted acrylic buffer. Fine dust lies in the rail groove, and the carriages show light scuffs. Everything is lined up.
end: The same rail has split at the switch point. The envelope with the acid-lime corner has thrown the lever as it passed, and behind it the thread has divided: some carriages run straight on, while others have swung onto a new branch that forks again and again, fanning into parallel tracks across the tabletop. Carriages are frozen mid-jump at each junction, envelopes lifting from their seats, one toppled on its side. None of the new tracks rejoins, and two run straight off the edge of the table. The frosted buffer at the end of the original line sits empty. Grinding marks and fine grey dust at the switch trace the split back to its origin.
apocalypse: A deep canyon of pale layered stone winds toward a bright gap on the horizon. Across it, the forked rails fan out as long derailed tracks, bent and snapped, some hanging from the rim into empty air, others lying twisted on the canyon floor among fallen rock. Graphite carriages the size of railcars lie on their sides, and weathered ivory envelopes, stiff and split, are wedged in crevices. The original switch point stands on a rock shelf, cracked through. Beside it, a slim graphite switching rig braced on outriggers has lifted the two nearest branches and is bolting them into one lime frog plate, and a lime rail joint leads onward along a single clean line across a repaired trestle.

title: @here broadcast
hero: frosted glass desk bell in a grid of desks
start: A grid of small brushed graphite desks sits in neat rows across a pale neutral tabletop, each desk the size of a matchbox and holding a small stack of ivory paper, a folded card or a frosted glass tumbler. On the front-left desk stands a small domed desk bell with a graphite base and a sandblasted frosted glass dome, its plunger a tiny acid-lime button. Every other desk carries an identical bell with a plain graphite plunger, unused. The desks are swept clean and aligned edge to edge. Light dust sits on the bell bases, and one paper stack shows a faint ring from a cup. The room is quiet and still.
end: The same grid of desks is shaking. The acid-lime plunger on the front-left bell is pressed down, and every bell across the grid has struck at once: domes are jumping off their bases, and fine lines of lifted dust ripple across the tabletop. Paper stacks slide off the desks and fan into the air, folded cards topple, and a frosted tumbler tips mid-fall, its rim chipping. One bell dome has cracked and is spinning on its edge. The desks have skated out of line, knocked askew in a pattern that spreads outward from the first desk, with the furthest ones pushed nearly to the table edge. Loose sheets hang frozen above the grid.
apocalypse: A broad tidal flat of pale grey mud stretches to a low sea line under an even sky, streaked with shallow channels. Enormous cracked bell domes of sandblasted frosted glass lie scattered across it, each as big as a chapel, tilted and half sunk, their milky surfaces stained. Graphite desks the size of barns lie flattened and thrown outward in rings from a single point, and ivory paper has crusted into the mud around them in weathered sheets. Long wind lines mark the mud between them. A slim graphite rig on wide tracks moves from dome to dome, lowering a lime clamp collar over each one to damp it; the nearest domes already wear lime collars and sit level and silent.

title: Channel sprawl
hero: frosted acrylic channel tray
start: A single shallow frosted acrylic tray about the size of a sheet of card rests at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop on four short graphite feet. Inside, a few small ivory message tiles float in a thin layer of clear water, drifting gently in one direction toward a graphite outlet lip. One tile carries an acid-lime edge, the thread everyone is following. Around the tray the tabletop is clear except for a folded ivory card and a small graphite scoop resting on its side. Light dust sits on the rim, and tiny ripples cross the water. Everything is calm, contained and orderly.
end: The same tray has split into dozens of near-identical shallow trays, cracking apart along new seams and spreading across the whole tabletop, some perched on others, some hanging over the edge. Water sloshes between them in frozen arcs, and the ivory message tiles are scattered across the network, stranded in the wrong trays, stuck to rims or flying through the air between them. The acid-lime tile has been flung into a small tray at the far edge, alone. Puddles spread across the table, the folded card is soaking and curling, and splash marks and a wet trail trace the spread back to the original tray.
apocalypse: A wide flooded basin stretches to a low line of hills, its shallow water still and grey, broken by the rims of hundreds of enormous sunken frosted trays, each the size of a field, their edges cracked and streaked with algae. Ivory message tiles the size of rafts float stranded in the wrong compartments or lie beached on the rims, swollen and softened. Pale silt lines on the tray walls show where the water has dropped. At the near edge, a slim graphite sorting flume on stilts runs out across the basin; its lime gates catch floating tiles and route them into a handful of clean channels, and a few recovered tiles already sit in neat rows at the flume's end.

title: Draft graveyard
hero: graphite outbox tray with frosted lid
start: A brushed graphite outbox tray about the size of a shoebox sits at the right of a pale neutral tabletop, with a hinged frosted acrylic lid. Under the half-open lid lies one half-finished ivory envelope, its flap unsealed and one corner slightly lifted. A short frosted glass flume leads out of the tray's front lip, dry and angled down toward a graphite send slot at the table edge. Beside the hinge, the tray's acid-lime send latch, a small lever, sits untouched. To the left lie a slim graphite pen and a single folded sheet. Fine dust gathers on the lid, and the envelope's edges show soft fibre. The scene is quiet and tidy.
end: The same outbox tray is jammed full. Unsent ivory drafts are stacked in crooked layers far above the rim, and the frosted lid is propped at an angle on top of the pile, unable to close, one hinge bent. Envelopes have slid down the pile and spilled out, some caught mid-fall off the tray's sides. The frosted flume is still dry, its mouth blocked by a wedged draft. The acid-lime send latch is untouched, pinned beneath the pile. Loose sheets have fanned across the table toward the pen, and fine paper dust drifts down from the overflow. Every spilled draft points back to the tray.
apocalypse: A dry, silted river channel winds between low eroded banks toward a distant drop, its floor packed with weathered ivory drafts compressed into grey paper silt and cracked into plates. Upstream, the outbox tray looms as a broken graphite reservoir wall, its frosted lid snapped and leaning against it like a fallen slab. The frosted flume runs along the channel as a long dry aqueduct, clogged at intervals with fused envelopes. Dust devils cross the far bank. Near the drop, a slim graphite pump rig has sunk a lime intake into the silt, and a lime pipe sends a steady stream of water down the flume; the first freed draft is tipping over the lip of the drop.

title: Per my last email
hero: nested printed email sheets
start: A single ivory printed sheet rests squarely at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, crisp, with blank grey bars standing in for lines of text. Folded beneath it and showing along its lower edge is a slightly smaller older sheet, and beneath that an even smaller one, each folded in thirds. A brushed graphite clip holds the stack together at the top. An acid-lime tab on the smallest, lowest sheet marks the original message. To the right, a frosted glass tray waits empty, and a graphite letter opener lies angled beside it. Light fibre fuzz shows along the folds. Everything is neat and flat.
end: The same printout has become a tower. Each sheet now holds a smaller copy of the last folded inside it, and the nested sheets have stacked into a tall, telescoping column rising above the graphite clip, each layer slightly offset and leaning. The column bows toward the frosted tray, and its upper layers are sliding off mid-fall, fanning into the air. The acid-lime tab on the original is buried at the base, just visible through a gap. The graphite clip has sprung open and is flying off to the left, and the letter opener has been knocked askew. Dog-eared edges and a haze of paper dust trace the leaning column back to the first sheet.
apocalypse: A range of rounded badland mounds stretches to a pale horizon, each built from collapsed nested paper tunnels: ivory sheets folded inside sheets, weathered grey and fused into crusted layers, with dark openings where tubes have caved in. Rain gullies score the slopes. On the nearest summit, the graphite clip rises as a twisted arch, and the frosted tray lies below it as a cracked basin filled with grit. At the base of the largest mound, a slim graphite boring rig stands on lime-legged footings, its long lime drill string driven straight into the slope; a clean core of neatly stacked sheets slides out onto a cradle beside it, ending in the small original sheet at its tip.

title: Accidental send
hero: spring-loaded graphite send lever
start: A small brushed graphite launch frame about the size of a stapler sits at the left of a pale neutral tabletop, with a coiled spring and a hinged send lever pulled back and held by a tiny catch. Resting in the lever's cup is one half-written ivory envelope, its flap open and an unfinished sheet sticking out. The catch is an acid-lime pin, the only thing holding the send. To the right, a row of small graphite recall hooks stands retracted on a rail. A plain graphite straightedge lies along the table's far side. Dust sits between the spring coils. The whole setup is still and cocked.
end: The same launch frame has fired early. The acid-lime pin has popped out and is spinning in the air above the frame, and the lever has snapped forward, flinging the half-written envelope in a high arc across the table, its loose sheet peeling out mid-flight. Behind it, the graphite recall hooks have sprung off their rail and are chasing it on extending arms, one closing on empty air, another snagged on the straightedge. The envelope is about to clear the far edge. Scattered dust, a skid mark under the frame's base and the recoil tilt of the spring trace the launch back to the left.
apocalypse: A grey crater field stretches to a flat horizon, pocked with shallow round impact pits, each holding a weathered ivory envelope driven nose-first into the ground, stiff, bleached and split along its folds. Fragments of graphite recall hooks the size of cranes lie bent across the crater rims. Far to the left, the launch frame stands as a weathered graphite ruin, its spring uncoiled and its lever thrown forward. Across the middle ground, a line of slim graphite masts has been driven into the ground, and a rig on a cable carriage is stringing a wide lime capture net between them, drawn taut on lime tensioners, closing off the field in front of the launch frame.

title: Unread counter
hero: graphite mechanical counter
start: A small mechanical counter about the size of a matchbox sits at the right of a pale neutral tabletop, housed in brushed graphite with chamfered corners. Through a narrow frosted glass window, four ivory counter wheels show plain blank faces with only faint tick marks. A graphite thumb lever on its side is at rest. At the left, a shallow graphite inbox tray holds a small, neat stack of ivory envelopes. On top of the counter, an acid-lime reset button, a small round cap, sits untouched. A fine film of dust covers the glass, and the tray shows light scuffs. Everything is quiet, and the stack is small.
end: The same counter is running out of control. Its ivory wheels spin in a blur behind the frosted window, and the graphite housing has split along one seam; one wheel has jumped its axle and is rolling across the tabletop, while small springs and pins spray out mid-air. The inbox tray at the left overflows with envelopes that pour over its sides and pile up around the counter's base, shoving it askew. The acid-lime reset button on top is still untouched. The thumb lever has snapped off and lies on the table. Paper dust and fine metal fragments hang frozen around the counter, and the envelope pile leads straight back to the tray.
apocalypse: A long slope of pale grey scree drops toward a wide, empty valley under a hazy sky. Scattered down it lie enormous ivory counter wheels, each as tall as a house, rolled free and resting on their edges or half buried in the loose stone, their faces blank and weathered. The graphite counter housing, split along its seam, sits at the top of the slope like a broken bunker, and drifts of weathered envelopes fill the gaps between rocks. Near the housing, a slim graphite rig on a short track has rolled one wheel back onto a lime axle cradle and is pulling a long lime reset lever; that first wheel now stands upright, level and aligned with the housing.

title: Signature attachment snowdrift
hero: envelope with clipped image tiles
start: One ivory envelope lies flat at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, crisp and blank, with a thin frosted acrylic reply card resting on top. Clipped to its lower edge by a small graphite clip are two tiny square image tiles of frosted acrylic, each blank and no bigger than a fingernail. One carries an acid-lime border, the attachment that actually matters. To the left sits an empty graphite letter tray, and to the right a slim folded ivory card. Fine fibres show at the envelope's edges, and light dust rests on the clip. The thread is simple and uncluttered.
end: The same envelope is disappearing under a snowdrift of tiny tiles. With each reply more blank frosted image tiles have clipped on, and now hundreds pour from the envelope's edges in a soft, sloping drift that covers the stacked reply cards and spreads across the tabletop toward the empty letter tray. Some tiles are caught mid-air, flicking up like snowflakes from the top of the pile. The acid-lime bordered tile is half buried near the base, only its lime edge visible. The folded card at the right has been knocked flat. A fine glittering dust of acrylic chips trails back to the graphite clip.
apocalypse: A high snowfield plateau of tiny weathered frosted tiles stretches to a white horizon, wind-packed into long ridged drifts with sharp cornices. From the nearest drift juts the corner of the envelope, now the size of a hangar, its ivory paper bleached, torn and frost-stiffened, the graphite clip still biting its edge like a fallen girder. The letter tray lies half buried in the middle distance, filled to the brim. A slim graphite sifter rig on skids works along the drift's edge, feeding tiles through a lime filter screen; the clutter falls through in a steady stream, and a cleaned strip of the envelope slides out onto a lime tray beside it.

title: File locked by another user
hero: card document folder with graphite padlock
start: A thick ivory card document folder about the size of a hardback book stands upright in a brushed graphite holder at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Its clasp is closed with a small graphite padlock whose body has a plain keyhole and whose acid-lime shackle is the one bright point in the scene, marking what is in the way. To the right, a single ivory copy of the folder waits on a short frosted acrylic shelf. A small graphite key hook on the holder hangs empty. The folder's edges show fibre and soft wear, and light dust sits on the shelf. Everything is orderly and still.
end: The same locked folder now has a queue. Ivory copies line the frosted shelf and spill beyond it in a long crooked row across the tabletop, each pushing on the one ahead. Graphite padlocks have snapped onto each copy's clasp, and more padlocks are dropping from above in mid-air, clamping onto the nearest edges and corners. The acid-lime shackle on the original is still closed. The frosted shelf has cracked under the weight, and copies near the end of the row are sliding off the table. Scrape marks, bent clasps and a haze of paper dust trace the queue back to the first folder.
apocalypse: A flat-topped mesa rises from a dusty plain under a pale sky, and on its summit sits a heap of weathered graphite padlocks the size of vehicles, fused together into a jagged hill, shackles interlocked and keyholes packed with grit. Ivory folders, bleached and warped into slabs, lean out of the heap at odd angles. The cracked frosted shelf juts from the mesa edge like a broken ledge. A slim graphite rig on articulated legs has climbed halfway into the heap; its lime master-key arm is turning inside one lock, the first shackle has sprung open, and a lime winch cable is pulling the freed folder clear onto a level platform.

title: Sync conflict copies
hero: frosted cloud canister and sync tube
start: A frosted acrylic canister shaped like a rounded cloud, about the size of a teapot, sits on a slim graphite stand at the upper left of a pale neutral tabletop, glowing softly inside. From its base, a single frosted glass tube runs down and across the table to a graphite document cradle at the lower right, where one ivory sheet rests. Midway along the tube, a small graphite valve sits with two capped side ports. Inside the tube, a rolled ivory document travels toward the cradle, wrapped in an acid-lime band. Dust rests on the stand's foot, and the cradle shows fine machining marks. Everything flows in one direction.
end: The same tube has jammed at the valve. A second rolled document has pushed up the tube from the cradle end and collided head-on with the acid-lime banded one, and both are crumpled at the junction. The capped side ports have burst open, and conflicted copies are branching into new side pipes that fork again across the tabletop, each carrying another ivory copy, some spilling out of open ends mid-air. Duplicate sheets are piling up around the cradle. The cloud canister is tilted on its stand, cracked along one seam. A puff of paper dust hangs over the junction, tracing the split back to the valve.
apocalypse: A wide river floodplain of pale gravel and flattened grass stretches to low hills. Across it, a collapsed aqueduct of giant frosted glass tubes lies in broken spans, its side pipes fanning out and sagging to the ground. Beneath, a field of duplicate ivory documents covers the plain like fallen leaves, weathered, stiffened and layered into grey drifts. The cloud canister lies on its side on a far hill, cracked open and silted. In the foreground, a slim graphite merge press on a rail cart is feeding stacks of duplicates between lime pressure plates, and a single compacted ivory document emerges onto a lime output tray, flat and clean.

title: Request access door
hero: frosted glass door with a request slot
start: A small frosted glass door about the height of a coffee mug stands in a brushed graphite frame at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Through the sandblasted glass, a single ivory document on a graphite stand shows as a soft blurred shape. Halfway up the door sits a narrow request slot with a graphite flap, and one small ivory request slip rests half inserted in it. The door's acid-lime handle, a short lever, is locked level. To the left, a small stack of blank slips waits on a graphite tray. Light dust gathers along the sill. The scene is quiet and closed.
end: The same door is still shut. Request slips have been pushed through the slot again and again; they jam its graphite flap open and pile into a deep, sloping heap against the door's base that spreads across the tabletop and pours over the edge. More slips are caught mid-air, fluttering from the tray at the left, which has tipped and emptied. The acid-lime handle has not moved. Behind the frosted glass, the document stands untouched and blurred. Creased slips, dented corners and a thin haze of paper dust trace the pile back to the slot.
apocalypse: A windswept mountain pass cuts between two grey ridges, its floor buried in deep drifts of weathered ivory request slips packed like old snow, curled and stiff, with wind-carved ripples. Straddling the pass, the graphite door frame stands as a massive weathered portal, the frosted glass door still shut but cracked and clouded, the blurred shape of the document just visible behind it. The slot at its middle is a dark, jammed opening. A slim graphite rig on tracked outriggers has dug a trench to the frame and is installing a lime gate mechanism beside the door, bolting lime hinge brackets into the frame; the new gate stands half open, framing a clean path through.

title: Comment pileup
hero: draft page on an easel with comment flags
start: An ivory draft page about the size of a postcard stands upright on a slim brushed graphite easel at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its surface lined with faint blank grey bars for text. Pinned into its right margin are three small comment flags, each a tiny ivory paper pennant on a graphite pin. The top flag has an acid-lime pennant, the one comment that matters. At the left sits a small frosted acrylic pin cushion holding a few spare pins, with a graphite pen beside it. Fine fibres show at the page's edge. Everything is spare and clear at a glance.
end: The same draft page is now a pincushion. Hundreds of ivory comment flags on graphite pins have been stuck into it, covering the margins and then the body until the grey bars have vanished. The page bows backward on its easel under the weight, torn around the densest clusters, and more flags are flying through the air toward it from the frosted cushion, which has been emptied and tipped over. Fallen flags lie scattered across the tabletop. The acid-lime pennant is buried deep in the cluster, only a sliver visible. Paper dust and bent pins trace the pile-up back to the margin.
apocalypse: A rolling heathland stretches to a distant ridge under a soft grey sky, and embedded across it lies the draft page, now the size of a valley floor, flattened into the ground and bleached. Thousands of comment flags as tall as trees stand in it, graphite pins leaning, ivory pennants faded and frayed into rags, with heather growing between them. The graphite easel lies toppled along the ridge like a fallen bridge. Through the middle, a slim graphite sweeper rig on wide rollers pulls flags out with lime tongs and stacks them on a lime trailer, leaving one clear lane of bare page that runs straight toward the ridge.

title: Markup sediment
hero: ivory page under frosted markup overlays
start: A clean ivory page about the size of a postcard lies flat at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its surface showing faint blank grey bars for text. Across one bar runs a single thin acid-lime strike line, the one tracked change. Beside it, a stack of thin frosted acrylic overlay sheets rests squarely on a brushed graphite tray, clear and unmarked. A graphite pen and a small graphite weight sit to the right. The page shows soft fibre and a crisp edge, and the overlays have milky bevelled edges. Light dust rests on the tray. Everything is flat, thin and orderly.
end: The same page is now buried under a thick translucent block. Overlay after overlay of frosted acrylic has been stacked on top, each carrying its own pale grey strike lines and margin marks, until the block is several fingers deep and the original page is barely visible through the milky layers. The stack is slipping off square, top sheets sliding sideways mid-motion and one overlay caught flying off the table edge. The acid-lime strike line glows faintly at the very bottom. The graphite tray is empty and pushed aside. Fine acrylic chips and dust trace the stack back to the page.
apocalypse: A tall sediment cliff rises along a dry riverbank, its face built from thousands of thin frosted acrylic markup layers compressed into milky bands, weathered and chipped, with erosion gullies cutting down it. At its base, fallen slabs lie in a talus of broken layers. The graphite tray protrudes from one band like a fossil shelf, and the graphite weight sits on the bank below as a rounded boulder. At the cliff foot, a slim graphite core drill rig on a lime tripod has bored horizontally into the lowest layer, and a lime sleeve is sliding out a clean core; at its end sits a small, intact ivory page.
